title: The worker that will not work
summary: The job queue keeps growing even though the worker process is still there.
briefing: Jobs are piling up in /srv/queue. The queue worker has not crashed: it is still in the process list, and restarting it is not allowed because it holds in-flight work. Find out why it is not consuming jobs and get the backlog down.

objectives.text: The original queue worker is running again (same PID, not stopped)
objectives.regressed: The worker is stopped again, or it was replaced. The goal was to resume the original process.

hints: `ls /srv/queue | wc -l` shows the backlog. `ps -eo pid,stat,args | grep queue` shows the worker and its state.
A STAT of T means the process is stopped by a signal. It exists but is never scheduled.
SIGSTOP cannot be caught or ignored. The matching signal to resume it is SIGCONT: `kill -CONT <pid>`.
debrief: A stopped process (state T) looks alive in every process list but does no work. SIGSTOP is how Ctrl+Z and debuggers pause programs, and it cannot be caught; only SIGCONT resumes it. Restarting would have lost in-flight work, while SIGCONT resumed the original process exactly where it paused. In production, a queue whose consumer is present but not consuming is a classic sign of a paused or deadlocked worker.
setup:
mkdir -p /opt/queue /srv/queue
cat > /opt/queue/worker <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
while true; do
  for f in /srv/queue/*.job; do
    [ -e "$f" ] && mv "$f" /srv/queue/.done
  done
  sleep 1
done
EOF
cat > /opt/queue/producer <<'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
while true; do
  touch "/srv/queue/$(date +%s%N).job"
  sleep 1
done
EOF
chmod +x /opt/queue/worker /opt/queue/producer
for i in $(seq 1 40); do touch "/srv/queue/backlog-$i.job"; done
setsid /opt/queue/worker >/dev/null 2>&1 </dev/null &
echo $! > /opt/queue/worker.pid
setsid /opt/queue/producer >/dev/null 2>&1 </dev/null &
sleep 0.5
kill -STOP "$(cat /opt/queue/worker.pid)"
sleep 1
